question.value: Does the turbulence (velocity dispersion) of galaxy disks evolve with cosmic time (z = 0-5) when measured from cold gas tracers, how does it compare with warm ionized gas measurements, and what drives it?

evidence.quote: Do the cold gas kinematics exhibit differences compared to warm counterparts when galaxies with similar physical properties are considered?
Does turbulence in disks evolve with cosmic time when measured from cold gas tracers?

evidence.quote: The models shown in Fig. [6](#fig:model) suggest only a mild redshift evolution of turbulence motion within the range $z = 0$ - 2 and no significant evolution at $z > 2$.

claims.hypothesis: Does cold-gas turbulence evolve strongly with redshift?
claims.experiment: Fit empirical sigma-z and V/sigma-z relations to the 57-galaxy extended sample (CO, [CI], [CII] kinematics)
claims.result: sigma rises by a factor ~2-3 over z = 0-1 and plateaus at z > 1; V/sigma shows the reverse
claims.finding: Disks are rotation-dominated across z = 0-5; trends reflect a heterogeneous sample

evidence.quote: There is a trend of $\sigma$ increasing by around 2 to 3 times across the redshift range $z = 0 - 1$

claims.hypothesis: Do warm (H-alpha) and cold gas kinematics agree for galaxies with similar properties?
claims.experiment: Compare medians in matched redshift bins with SAMI, DYNAMO, Hogan+21 and KAOSS samples
claims.result: H-alpha sigma is higher and V/sigma lower than cold gas by about a factor of 3
claims.finding: Warm gas kinematics are not equivalent to cold gas kinematics; cause not identified

evidence.quote: we cannot determine what is causing the discrepancy between warm and cold gas kinematics

claims.hypothesis: Is cold-gas turbulence driven by gravitational instabilities (disk-instability model) or by stellar feedback?
claims.experiment: Compare the data with the Wisnioski disk-instability model and with K18 feedback and transport models in the sigma-SFR plane
claims.result: The disk-instability model overestimates sigma by 2-4; data follow feedback models
claims.finding: Stellar feedback can reproduce cold-gas turbulence

evidence.quote: gravitational instabilities tend to overpredict turbulence measured from cold gas

claims.hypothesis: A supernova-driven model with sigma proportional to SFR^(1/3) describes the sigma-SFR relation and predicts turbulence evolution
claims.experiment: Fit log sigma-log SFR with slope fixed at 0.33 and compare with free slope, then combine with main-sequence evolution
claims.result: intercept 0.77 +/- 0.03 with 0.13 dex scatter; free slope 0.27 +/- 0.03; model agrees with data
claims.finding: Turbulence evolution follows the main-sequence evolution; driving physics does not evolve

evidence.quote: This is another confirmation of the supernova-driven nature of the turbulence.

why_this_data.value: No systematic high-resolution CO surveys exist at z = 0.5-4, so ALMA archival data mined for ALPAKA are combined with literature

evidence.quote: there have been no high-resolution systematic surveys of CO at $z = 0.5 - 4$, but only observations of single targets

why_this_method.value: F21 model chosen for its few free parameters rather than the K18 models

evidence.quote: The F21 model has fewer free parameters, enabling us to better control and understand their impact on the results.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Slopes of 0.5 and 1 for the sigma-SFR relation (momentum-based) were fitted and rejected; only 0.33 reproduces the data

evidence.quote: the relation with a slope of $m = 0.33$ is the only one that accurately reproduces the data

referee_caveats_inferred: Sample is heterogeneous in selection, tracers (CO, [CI], [CII]) and per-paper 3DBarolo analysis, so sigma values are not measured uniformly
[CII] sigma at z > 4 may include contributions from non-molecular gas
Cold vs warm comparison uses different galaxies and mostly medians, not matched sources
The sigma-SFR slope of 0.33 is partly assumed (fixed) and the CC constancy argument relies on rough order-of-magnitude values
High-z sigma near the spectral resolution (~30 km/s) may bias the sigma-z plateau
